business.title: Point-of-care hearing screening using consumer wireless earbuds in patients with USH2A-associated retinal disease: a prospective pilot feasibility study
business.description: Usher syndrome type 2 (USH2) may be under-recognized in ophthalmology practice due to variable hearing loss severity and limited point-of-care audiometry. In this prospective pilot study at the Singapore National Eye Centre (November 2024 to February 2025) we evaluated a consumer earbud hearing test in patients with USH2A-associated retinal disease and explored cross-sectional relationships between hearing and visual measures. Thirteen patients with biallelic USH2A pathogenic variants (median age 45 years, range 29-81) and thirteen age- and sex-matched comparison participants underwent supervised air-conduction threshold estimation using AirPods Pro 2. All participants completed testing without failure, repetition or technical error. Among patients, median test duration was 4.5 minutes (range 3.6–5.1), and three required physical guidance. These feasibility outcomes are reported descriptively and post hoc. Right-ear pure-tone average (PTA4-R) ranged from 13.00 to 84.25 dB HL (median 48.25 dB HL) and ellipsoid zone (EZ) width ranged from 0 to 7,972 μm (median 1,037 μm). After adjustment for age, higher PTA4-R showed a negative association estimate with EZ width (β = −57.36 μm/dB, 95% CI −117.56 to 2.83; nominal p = 0.0597) and a positive association estimate with best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in logMAR units (β = 0.02793 logMAR/dB, 95% CI 0.00429 to 0.05156; nominal p = 0.0251). Neither met the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold (adjusted p = 0.1194 and 0.0501, respectively). Earbud-derived threshold configurations resembled previously described USH2A-associated patterns, but agreement with calibrated clinical audiometry was not assessed. Formal audiological evaluation remains necessary for diagnosis and management.

science.title: Parents’ perceptions of high-quality nursing care for children with cancer: a qualitative descriptive study
science.description: Parents remain closely involved in caring for children hospitalized with cancer, yet nursing quality extends beyond clinical task performance. Although previous studies have identified important aspects of pediatric oncology nursing care, less is known about how parents integrate these dimensions when evaluating overall care quality. To describe parents’ perceptions of high-quality nursing care for children hospitalized with cancer and explore how these dimensions shape parental confidence in care reliability. A qualitative descriptive study was conducted in a pediatric oncology ward in Sanandaj, Iran. Sixteen parents (14 mothers and two fathers) participated in semi-structured interviews, and seven completed follow-up interviews, resulting in 23 interview encounters. Data were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis. Reflexive notes, field notes, an audit trail, collaborative analytic review, and participant follow-up supported trustworthiness. Five interconnected categories were identified: building a respectful and responsive care relationship; demonstrating clinical vigilance and technical competence; providing emotional security and child-centered support; enabling parental caregiving through practical education; and organizational conditions constraining reliable care. Parents evaluated nursing quality through the interaction of these dimensions. Parental confidence emerged as an integrated interpretation reflecting perceptions of care as safe, responsive, individualized, and dependable. Confidence was challenged when parents perceived workload pressures, overcrowding, staffing concerns, or variability in expertise as affecting care consistency. Parent-perceived nursing quality in pediatric oncology was described as multidimensional, reflecting parents’ perceptions of interactions between nursing practices and contextual conditions. Future quality-improvement efforts may consider communication, competence, emotional support, education, and organizational factors that parents perceive as influencing reliable care delivery.
